title: Bījak
genre: Sant song anthology (scripture of the Kabīr Chaurā line)

attribution.tradition: Kabīr's own words, compiled by his disciple Bhāgodās (Bhagvān Dās)
attribution.scholarly: the eastern recension of the Kabīr corpus; many verses are later additions in Kabīr's name; manuscripts are late (18th–19th c.)

tradition.text: Kabīr's lifetime (1398–1518 in the panth's reckoning)

scholarly.text: compiled in the Kabīr Panth, probably 17th c. or later; oldest dated manuscripts late

structure.description: Sections: Ramainī (84), Śabda (115), Jñān Cauṃtīsā, Vipramatīsī, Kaharā (12), Basant (12), Cācar (2), Belī (2), Birahulī, Hiṇḍolā (3), Sākhī (353) — counts as in the Shukdev Singh edition; other editions differ

summary: The Bījak ('treasure-map, inventory') is the scripture of the Kabīr Chaurā line: ramainīs on creation, māyā and delusion; śabdas that satirize paṇḍit and mullā, yogī and ascetic, and call the sants to see; sākhī couplets on the Word, the guru, death and discernment (pārakh). Its tone is sharply critical and apophatic, stressing testing and discernment over devotional sweetness.

editions.name: L. Hess & Shukdev Singh, The Bījak of Kabir (1983)
with Viśvanāth Siṃh's Pākhaṇḍ-khaṇḍinī commentary (19th c.)

notes: Section counts are from memory (moderate confidence); the sākhī count in particular varies by edition (353 in Shukdev Singh).

title: Kabīr Granthāvalī

attribution.tradition: Kabīr's sākhīs and padas as preserved in Rajasthani (Dādūpanthī) manuscripts
attribution.scholarly: the western recension; the Dādūpanthī manuscripts (from c. 1600 onward) are among the oldest witnesses of Kabīr; editions by Śyāmsundar Dās (1928) and Pārasnāth Tivārī (1961)

scholarly.text: manuscripts from c. 1600 (Fatehpur 1582 manuscript of Sūr and others; Dādūpanthī Pañcvāṇī manuscripts 17th c.)

structure.description: Sākhīs arranged in some 59 aṅgas (topics: gurudev, sumiraṇ, birah, gyān-birah, paracā, ras, jarṇā, hairān, lai, nihakarmī-pativratā, citāvaṇī, man, māyā, sahaj, sāṃc, bhram-bidhauṃsaṇ, bheṣ, saṅgati, sādh, madhi, sārgrāhī, sabad, jīvan-mṛtak, sūrātan, kāl, kastūriyā-mṛg, nindā, bīnatī, belī, etc.), padas (some 400) in rāgas, and ramainīs

summary: The western (Rajasthani) collection of Kabīr, arranged by topic (aṅg) as in the Dādūpanthī anthologies: the guru, remembrance of the Name, the pain of separation, the encounter (paracā) with the Beloved, the mind, māyā, the sahaj state, the true sādhu, the valour of the spiritual warrior and death. It is warmer in devotional tone than the Bījak.

editions.name: Kabīr Granthāvalī, ed. Śyāmsundar Dās (Nāgarīpracāriṇī Sabhā, Kāśī, 1928)
Ch. Vaudeville, Kabīr (1974), vol. 1 (translation of the sākhīs)

notes: Number of aṅgas (59) and padas (c. 400) from memory; aṅga names given where recalled (moderate-to-low confidence on each).

title: The oral and popular corpus of Kabīr (sākhīs, dohās, padas and bhajans)
alt_titles: Kabīr Vacanāvalī (Hariaudh's anthology, 1916) and similar anthologies
Kṣitimohan Sen's collection 'Kabīr' (Bengali script, 1910–11), basis of Tagore's Songs of Kabir (1915)

attribution.tradition: all ascribed to Kabīr by singers, panths and schoolbooks
attribution.scholarly: a living, growing corpus; many famous dohās are absent from the oldest recensions, and much of Kṣitimohan Sen's collection (hence Tagore's Songs of Kabir) is of doubtful authenticity

summary: The couplets and songs everyone quotes as Kabīr's — on reading and love, the musk-deer, the guru and Govind, the mill-stones, the mind, stone idols and the mullā's call — sung in bhajan and Kabīr Panth gatherings and printed in anthologies. The ontology records them as the tradition's Kabīr, with the attribution marked disputed.

editions.name: R. Tagore (with E. Underhill), Songs of Kabir (1915)

notes: Created by this unit as the honest home for teachings whose attribution is popular rather than critical; each teaching notes whether the verse is also found in the Bījak or Granthāvalī when recalled.

title: Ādi Granth (Guru Granth Sāhib)

attribution.tradition: compiled by Guru Arjan (1604) with the hymns of the Sikh Gurus and of bhagats including Kabīr, Ravidās, Nāmdev, Pīpā, Sain, Dhannā, Trilocan, Beṇī, Sadhnā, Farīd, Jaidev, Sūrdās, Paramānand and Rāmānand
attribution.scholarly: the earliest securely dated written witness (1604) for Kabīr, Ravidās and Nāmdev

tradition.text: compiled 1604; the final recension (with Guru Tegh Bahādur's hymns) 1706

summary: CONTEXT ONLY — Sikh scripture is outside this ontology's scope. Recorded because it preserves the Punjabi recension of Kabīr (over 500 verses), 40 hymns and a couplet of Ravidās and hymns of Nāmdev and other Sant bhagats; the Ravidāsī tradition drew its scripture from these hymns until 2010.
notes: Context only (U27 brief: Sikh scripture outside scope). No Sikh teachings are extracted; Sant hymns preserved here are recorded under the Sants' own source ids (e.g. src:ravidas-bani) with the Ādi Granth as location.

title: Anurāg Sāgar

attribution.scholarly: a Dharamdāsī text, probably 18th c.

summary: Kabīr tells Dharamdās how the Sat Puruṣ emanated sixteen sons; how Kāl Nirañjan won by austerity the three worlds and the goddess Ādyā (Aṣṭāṅgī), from whom Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheś were born; how Kāl traps souls in the round of births; and how Kabīr, in each age, comes to lead souls (haṃs) back to Satlok through the true Name. It also prophesies the Dharamdāsī line of forty-two generations.

editions.name: The Ocean of Love: The Anurag Sagar of Kabir (Sant Bani Ashram, 1982)

title: Kabīr Sāgar

attribution.tradition: Kabīr's teaching preserved in the Dharamdāsī line
attribution.scholarly: a compilation of Dharamdāsī texts (Jñān Sāgar, Anurāg Sāgar, Amar Mūl and others), published in the early 20th c. (ed. Swāmī Yugalānanda)

summary: The large collection of the Dharamdāsī Kabīr Panth, containing the Anurāg Sāgar and many other dialogues (sāgars and bodhs) on cosmogony, the Name, initiation and the lineage.
notes: Number of volumes and exact contents not recalled with confidence.

title: Kabīr Paracaī

attribution.tradition: by Anantadās of the Rāmānandī lineage
attribution.scholarly: c. 1588 (Lorenzen); the earliest extended life of Kabīr

summary: The earliest connected account of Kabīr's life: the weaver of Banaras who receives Rāmānanda's teaching, is persecuted by brahmins, qāzīs and Sultan Sikandar Lodī, survives ordeals, and at death goes to Maghar.

editions.name: D. N. Lorenzen, Kabir Legends and Ananta-das's Kabir Parachai (1991)

title: Raidās Paracaī

attribution.scholarly: late 16th c.

summary: Anantadās's life of Raidās: the leatherworker devotee of Banaras, his humility and poverty, the brahmins' hostility, the proof of his sanctity and the queen of Chittor (Jhālī) who becomes his disciple.

editions.name: W. M. Callewaert & P. G. Friedlander, The Life and Works of Raidās (1992)

title: Bījak Trijyā (commentary of Pūran Sāhib)

attribution.scholarly: early 19th c. commentary; basis of the 'Pārakh' (discernment) interpretation

summary: A Kabīr Panth commentary on the Bījak that reads it as a manual of discernment (pārakh): the seeker tests every doctrine and deity, recognizing them as products of the mind, until only the discerning self remains.

title: Pākhaṇḍ-khaṇḍinī (commentary on the Bījak)

attribution.tradition: by Mahārāj Viśvanāth Siṃh of Rewā
attribution.scholarly: 19th c.; reads Kabīr's Rām in a Rāma-bhakti sense

summary: A royal commentary on the Bījak, 'the destroyer of hypocrisy', which reads Kabīr's critique of outward religion within a Vaiṣṇava Rāma-bhakti frame.

title: Kabīr–Gorakh Goṣṭhī

attribution.tradition: a debate between Kabīr and Gorakhnāth
attribution.scholarly: a Kabīr Panth text of uncertain (late) date; the meeting is legendary (the two are not contemporaries on any scholarly chronology)

summary: A dialogue staging a debate between Kabīr and Gorakhnāth, in which Kabīr's devotion to the Name and the inner guru is shown surpassing the yogī's practices (shared with U21).

title: Pañcvāṇī

attribution.tradition: Dādūpanthī anthology of five saints: Dādū, Kabīr, Nāmdev, Ravidās and Hardās
attribution.scholarly: 17th c. manuscripts; a principal witness to the western Kabīr and Nāmdev

summary: The Dādūpanthī anthology of 'five voices' — Dādū, Kabīr, Nāmdev, Ravidās and Hardās — copied for use in the panth; a key early witness for the Sant corpus.

editions.name: W. M. Callewaert, The Millennium Kabīr Vāṇī (2000) uses Pañcvāṇī manuscripts

title: Sarbaṅgī (Sarvāṅgī) of Rajjab

attribution.tradition: compiled by Rajjab, disciple of Dādū
attribution.scholarly: early 17th c.

summary: Rajjab's anthology of verses from many saints (Sant and others) arranged by spiritual topic (aṅg), showing the Dādūpanthī sense of a single teaching running through all the saints.

title: Sarvāṅgī of Gopāldās

attribution.scholarly: dated 1627

summary: A Dādūpanthī anthology of verses of many saints arranged by topic, an important early witness of Kabīr and other Sants.

editions.name: W. M. Callewaert, The Sarvāṅgī of Gopāldās (1993)

title: Bāṇī of Ravidās (Raidās kī Bāṇī)

attribution.scholarly: 40 hymns and 1 couplet in the Ādi Granth (1604) plus Rajasthani manuscript songs; authenticity of the later songs debated

structure.description: 40 śabads and 1 śaloka in the Ādi Granth, in 16 rāgas; further padas and sākhīs in Rajasthani manuscripts (Callewaert & Friedlander edit c. 100 songs)

summary: The songs of Ravidās: the city without sorrow (Begampura); the Lord who raises the low-born; his own caste of leatherworkers who carry dead cattle round Banaras; the unity of self and God like gold and bracelet; and the offering of the mind when every outward offering is already defiled.

editions.name: W. M. Callewaert & P. G. Friedlander, The Life and Works of Raidās (1992)

title: Amritbāṇī Satguru Ravidās Mahārāj

attribution.tradition: the hymns of Guru Ravidās compiled as scripture by Dera Sachkhand Ballan
attribution.scholarly: compiled and declared 2010

summary: The scripture of the Ravidassia Dharam declared by Dera Sachkhand Ballan in 2010, containing Ravidās's hymns (drawn largely from the Ādi Granth recension) for use in Ravidāsī places of worship in place of the Guru Granth Sāhib.

title: Dādū Vāṇī (Dādū Dayāl kī Bāṇī)

attribution.tradition: Dādū's utterances, arranged by Rajjab in aṅgas
attribution.scholarly: compiled shortly after 1603; broadly authentic

structure.description: Some 2,600 sākhīs in 37 aṅgas (from Gurudev kau aṅg, Sumiran kau aṅg, Birah kau aṅg, Paracā kau aṅg … to Abihaṛ kau aṅg) and some 440 padas in 27 rāgas (approximate counts)

summary: Dādū's sākhīs and songs on the guru met in the unseen, remembrance of Rām, separation and encounter, the body as the true mosque and temple, impartiality between Hindu and Turk, the middle way, and dying to self while alive. It opens with an invocation to Nirañjan, the gurudev and all sādhus.

editions.name: Dādū Dayāl kī Bāṇī (Belvedere Press, Allahabad; Santbānī series)
Śrī Dādū Vāṇī, ed. Svāmī Nārāyaṇdās (Jaipur)

title: Dādū Janma Līlā

attribution.scholarly: early 17th c.

summary: The life of Dādū by his disciple Jangopāl: his appearance at Ahmedabad, the old man (Buḍḍhan) who blesses him, his life as a cotton-carder at Sambhar and Amer, his audience with Akbar at Fatehpur Sikri (1585) and his death at Naraina.

editions.name: W. M. Callewaert, The Hindī Biography of Dādū Dayāl (1988)

title: Rajjab kī Vāṇī
summary: Rajjab's own verse on the guru, the Name and renunciation, by the Pathan disciple who left his wedding procession to follow Dādū.

title: Jñān Samudra (Gyān Samudra)

attribution.scholarly: dated 1653 (moderate confidence)

structure.description: five ullāsas: the guru and disciple; bhakti (navadhā and premā); yoga (haṭha and aṣṭāṅga); sāṃkhya; advaita (approximate)

summary: Sundardās's learned exposition of the Sant path in Braj verse as a dialogue of guru and disciple, moving through devotion, yoga and Sāṃkhya to non-dual knowledge — a Sant teaching in the categories of Sanskrit śāstra.

title: Sundar Vilās
summary: Sundardās's polished savaiyā poems by topic (the guru, the mind, the body, knowledge, the ignorant, the sādhu), celebrated for literary finish.

title: Sundar Granthāvalī

attribution.scholarly: ed. Purohit Harinārāyaṇ Śarmā (1936)

summary: The collected works of Sundardās (some forty-two small works plus Jñān Samudra and Sundar Vilās).

title: Malūkdās kī Bānī

attribution.tradition: the verses of Malūkdās of Kaṛā
attribution.scholarly: printed in the Belvedere Press Santbānī series; works named Ratnakhān and Gyānbodh are attributed (low confidence)

summary: Malūkdās's sayings and songs of trust in Rām's providence ('the python does no service, the bird does no work…'), of the inner Rām and of equal regard for all.

title: Paltū Sāhib kī Bānī

attribution.tradition: the verses of Paltū Sāhib of Ayodhyā
attribution.scholarly: Belvedere Press edition in three parts

summary: Paltū's forceful verses against hypocrisy and for the inner Name and sound; much used in Sant Mat literature.

title: Dariyā Sāgar
summary: The principal work of Dariyā Sāhib of Bihar on the Name, the inner sound and the path to Satlok.

title: Bānī of Dariyā Sāhib of Mārvāṛ

attribution.tradition: verses of Dariyāv Sāhib of Rain

summary: The verses of the Marwari Dariyā (Dariyāv) Sāhib of Rain, founder of a Rāmsnehī seat, on remembrance of Rām and the inner sound.

title: Bhakti Sāgar (collected works of Caraṇdās)

attribution.scholarly: includes treatises on bhakti, aṣṭāṅga yoga and brahmajñāna (low confidence on titles)

summary: Caraṇdās's collected works joining devotion to Kṛṣṇa and the guru with aṣṭāṅga yoga and knowledge of Brahman.

title: Sahaj Prakāś

attribution.scholarly: dated 1743 (moderate confidence)

summary: Sahajobāī's verses exalting the guru above Hari, on the sahaj path, the Name, death and detachment.

title: Dayā Bodh

attribution.tradition: by Dayābāī, disciple of Caraṇdās (a 'Vinay Mālikā' is also attributed)

summary: Dayābāī's verses on devotion to the guru, love and separation, and the Name.

title: Garībdās jī kī Bāṇī (Granth Sāhib of Garībdās)

attribution.tradition: the utterances of Garībdās of Chhuḍānī

summary: The large verse corpus of Garībdās, which exalts Kabīr as the supreme God and describes Satlok, the Name and the lineage of true saints.

title: Jagjīvan Sāhib kī Bānī
summary: Verses of the Satnāmī founder Jagjīvandās on the true Name and the formless Lord.

title: Vāṇī of Haridās Nirañjanī
summary: Verses of the founder of the Nirañjanī sampradāya on Nirañjan, yoga and devotion.

title: Aṇbhai Vāṇī
summary: The collected verse of Rāmcaraṇ, founder of the Shāhpurā Rāmsnehīs, on remembrance of Rām and direct experience (aṇbhai).

title: Ghaṭ Rāmāyaṇ

attribution.tradition: by Tulsī Sāhib of Hāthras, who presents himself as having been Tulsīdās in a former life
attribution.scholarly: early 19th c.; authorship and integrity debated

summary: Tulsī Sāhib's 'Rāmāyaṇa of the body (ghaṭ)', which interprets the Rāma story as the inner journey of the soul and describes the inner regions and sounds above the eyes, anticipating the Radhasoami cosmology.

title: Ratan Sāgar
summary: Tulsī Sāhib's verse treatise on creation, the soul's descent and the path of return by the sound.

title: Sār Bachan (Sār Bachan Nazm and Sār Bachan Nasr)

scholarly.text: compiled after 1878 from Soamiji's discourses and poems

summary: The scripture of Radhasoami: in verse (Nazm) and prose (Nasr), Soamiji teaches that Radhasoami is the supreme being, that the soul (surat) is a drop of that ocean fallen into the regions of Kāl and māyā, and that it returns by surat-śabd yoga under a Sant Satguru through Sahasdal Kanwal, Trikuṭī, Sunn, Mahāsunn, Bhanwar Guphā and Sat Lok to Radhasoami Dhām.

title: Prem Patra (Radhasoami)
summary: Rai Salig Ram's letters and discourses (published in several volumes) expounding Radhasoami as the highest faith, the grades of creation and the practice of the sound current.

title: Discourses on Radhasoami Faith
summary: Brahm Shankar Misra's systematic English exposition of Radhasoami: the grand divisions of creation, spirit, mind and matter, and the path of the sound current.

title: Gurmat Siddhānt (tr. Philosophy of the Masters)
summary: Sawan Singh's exposition of Sant Mat through the Sant and Sikh scriptures: the Word (śabd), the Name, the Master, the inner regions and the practice.

title: Spiritual Gems
summary: Sawan Singh's letters to Western disciples on practice, karma, the inner regions, diet and the Master.

title: The Path of the Masters
summary: An American disciple's English presentation of Sant Mat as taught at Beas under Sawan Singh: the Master, the audible life stream, the five regions and the three bodies.

title: Die to Live
summary: Charan Singh's answers to disciples on 'dying while living' by meditation on the sound current, karma, the Master and diet.

title: Naam or Word
summary: Kirpal Singh's comparative exposition of the Word (Nām, śabd, logos, kalma) as the power that creates and sustains, heard within as sound and seen as light.

title: The Crown of Life
summary: Kirpal Singh's comparison of the yogas (haṭha, rāja, jñāna, bhakti, karma, laya) with surat-śabd yoga, presented as the crown of them all.

title: Satsaṅg Yog
summary: Maharshi Mehi's compilation of passages from the Upaniṣads, the Gītā and the Sants with his own exposition, to show that Santmat is their common teaching of inner light and sound.

title: Lālan-gīti (the songs of Lalon Fakir)
genre: Bāul songs (oral; later notebooks and printed collections)

attribution.tradition: the songs of Lalon Sāṃi, each signed with his and his guru Sirāj Sāṃi's name
attribution.scholarly: several hundred songs; transmitted orally and in disciples' notebooks; the Shilaidaha notebook used by Rabindranath Tagore's circle is an early written witness; authenticity of individual songs varies

summary: Lalon's songs ask where the unknown bird comes and goes in the cage of the body, long for union with the Man of the Heart, mock the question of caste, place the original Mecca in the human body, call the neighbour in the mirror-city whom one never sees, and urge worship of the human through the guru. They are the classic corpus of Bāul teaching.

editions.name: Lālan-gītikā, ed. Matilāl Dās & Pīyūṣkānti Mahāpātra (Calcutta University, 1958)
songs printed in Prabāsī (Hārāmaṇi section) from the Shilaidaha collection

title: Bāul gān (the corpus of Bāul songs of other masters)

attribution.tradition: songs signed (bhaṇitā) by Bāul and Fakir masters: Madan, Gagan Harkarā, Duddu Śāh, Pāñju Śāh, Pāglā Kānāi, Jādubindu and many others
attribution.scholarly: oral; partial written collections from the late 19th c. (Tagore's circle, Muhammad Mansuruddin's Hārāmaṇi, Upendranāth Bhaṭṭācārya's Bāṃlār Bāul o Bāul Gān, 1957)

summary: The living song corpus of the Bāuls beyond Lalon: songs of the Man of the Heart, the body, the guru and the path, and of the futility of temple and mosque.

title: Hārāmaṇi
genre: collection of folk and Bāul songs

attribution.tradition: the 'lost jewels' of Bengali folk song collected by Muhammad Mansuruddin
attribution.scholarly: 13 volumes from 1931

summary: Muhammad Mansuruddin's great collection of Bengali folk songs including many Bāul and Lalon songs, a principal printed witness for the oral corpus.

title: Phikir Cāṃder Bāul Saṅgīt

attribution.tradition: songs of Kāṅgāl Harināth under the pen-name Phikir Cāṃd

summary: Songs in the Bāul manner by Harināth Majumdar and his troupe, including 'hari din to gela, sandhyā holo, pār karo āmāre'.

title: Hāsan Udās

attribution.scholarly: published 1907 (moderate confidence)

summary: Hāsan Rājā's songs of detachment from house and wealth and of the soul as a caged bird, in the Sylheti mystic-song idiom akin to the Bāuls'.

title: Amṛtaratnāvalī

attribution.scholarly: post-Caitanya, 17th–18th c.; manuscripts edited in part by M. M. Basu and others

summary: A principal Sahajiyā manual attributed to Mukunda Dāsa: the sahaja mānuṣa within, the distinction of rūpa and svarūpa, the practice of āropa, the stages of the path and the ideal of parakīyā love (in coded language).
notes: Existence recalled from the scholarly literature (M. M. Basu, S. B. Dasgupta, E. C. Dimock); contents only in outline.

title: Āgamasāra

attribution.scholarly: post-Caitanya, 17th–18th c.; manuscripts edited in part by M. M. Basu and others

summary: A Sahajiyā text on the sahaja principle and the body as the place of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, in dialogue form (authorship not recalled).
notes: Existence recalled from the scholarly literature (M. M. Basu, S. B. Dasgupta, E. C. Dimock); contents only in outline.

title: Ānandabhairava

attribution.scholarly: post-Caitanya, 17th–18th c.; manuscripts edited in part by M. M. Basu and others

summary: A Sahajiyā text, perhaps framed as a dialogue of deities, on rasa and the sahaja path (low confidence on content).
notes: Existence recalled from the scholarly literature (M. M. Basu, S. B. Dasgupta, E. C. Dimock); contents only in outline.

title: Amṛtarasāvalī

attribution.scholarly: post-Caitanya, 17th–18th c.; manuscripts edited in part by M. M. Basu and others

summary: A Sahajiyā text on the nectar of rasa and the stages of the sahaja path (attributed in some accounts to Mukunda's circle; low confidence).
notes: Existence recalled from the scholarly literature (M. M. Basu, S. B. Dasgupta, E. C. Dimock); contents only in outline.

title: Vivartavilāsa

attribution.scholarly: post-Caitanya, 17th–18th c.; manuscripts edited in part by M. M. Basu and others

summary: Akiñcana Dāsa's Sahajiyā work, which reads the Caitanya-caritāmṛta and the Gosvāmīs' teaching as esoteric Sahajiyā doctrine and claims Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja for the Sahajiyā lineage.
notes: Existence recalled from the scholarly literature (M. M. Basu, S. B. Dasgupta, E. C. Dimock); contents only in outline.

title: Ratnasāra (Sahajiyā)

attribution.scholarly: post-Caitanya, 17th–18th c.; manuscripts edited in part by M. M. Basu and others

summary: A Sahajiyā manual on the sahaja mānuṣa and the stages of practice (low confidence on author and date).
notes: Existence recalled from the scholarly literature (M. M. Basu, S. B. Dasgupta, E. C. Dimock); contents only in outline.

title: Bhṛṅgaratnāvalī

attribution.scholarly: post-Caitanya, 17th–18th c.; manuscripts edited in part by M. M. Basu and others

summary: A Sahajiyā text attributed to Mukunda Dāsa on the lotuses and lakes of the inner body and the bee (bhṛṅga) of the mind (low confidence).
notes: Existence recalled from the scholarly literature (M. M. Basu, S. B. Dasgupta, E. C. Dimock); contents only in outline.

title: Rāgamayīkaṇā

attribution.scholarly: post-Caitanya, 17th–18th c.; manuscripts edited in part by M. M. Basu and others

summary: A Sahajiyā text on rāga (passionate love) as the way (low confidence).
notes: Existence recalled from the scholarly literature (M. M. Basu, S. B. Dasgupta, E. C. Dimock); contents only in outline.

title: Nigūḍhārtha-prakāśāvalī

attribution.scholarly: post-Caitanya, 17th–18th c.; manuscripts edited in part by M. M. Basu and others

summary: A Sahajiyā text 'revealing the hidden meaning' of Vaiṣṇava doctrine in the Sahajiyā sense (low confidence).
notes: Existence recalled from the scholarly literature (M. M. Basu, S. B. Dasgupta, E. C. Dimock); contents only in outline.

title: Rāgātmikā padas of the Sahajiyā Caṇḍīdās

attribution.tradition: songs of Caṇḍīdās, lover of the washerwoman Rāmī
attribution.scholarly: the 'Caṇḍīdās problem': several poets used the name (Baḍu Caṇḍīdās of the Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtan, Dvija and Dīna Caṇḍīdās); the Sahajiyā padas are generally later

tradition.text: the tradition places Caṇḍīdās before Caitanya (who is said to have enjoyed his songs)

summary: The songs ascribed to the Sahajiyā Caṇḍīdās: 'Listen, brother man — the truth of man is above all, nothing is above it'; everyone speaks of sahaja but who knows it?; the washerwoman's love is tested gold without a trace of lust.

title: Bhāber Gīt
alt_titles: Songs of Bhāva / Songs of Ecstasy

attribution.tradition: the songs of Dulālcānd (Rāmdulāl Pāl), son of Rāmśaraṇ Pāl and Satī Mā
attribution.scholarly: early 19th c.; printed from 1870 onward in editions of several hundred songs

summary: The Kartābhajā songs, deliberately obscure, which describe the Master's hidden presence, the sahaja mānuṣa, and the spiritual trade of the soul in the imagery of Calcutta's bazaars, companies, ships and merchandise.

editions.name: H. B. Urban, Songs of Ecstasy (2001) — selections

title: Kartābhajā sayings and maxims (oral)

attribution.tradition: maxims transmitted among Kartābhajā gurus (Mahāśay) and disciples (barātī)
attribution.scholarly: recorded in 19th–20th c. writings and ethnographies

summary: The maxims of the Kartābhajā: 'in the world, worldly custom; with the true guru, oneness'; 'the guru is truth'; 'worship the human'. Created by this unit as the home for sayings whose written locus is not recalled.

title: Sahajatattva-prakāśa (Kartābhajā dharmer ādi vṛttānta)

attribution.tradition: by Manulāl Miśra, a Kartābhajā Mahāśay
attribution.scholarly: early 20th c. (c. 1911)

summary: A Kartābhajā insider's account of the sect's origins (Āulcānd, Rāmśaraṇ, Satī Mā) and exposition of the sahaja doctrine and the worship of the Kartā.
